job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here are the issues in bill order. I've marked the four I'd treat as must-fix before Thursday with **[critical]**. This is a review of the text only. Legislative counsel should confirm the drafting fixes, and staff should verify the current status of any pending DSHMRA applications or ISA contracts before relying on specifics.

1. **§7(b) vs. §7(a) [critical].** §7(b) ends the entire Act 10 years after enactment, but §7(a) keeps the prohibition in place only until Congress passes a joint resolution. Read literally, the prohibition expires in a decade unless Congress acts, which reverses the bill's purpose. Delete the sunset or convert it into a required review.

2. **§5(a) vs. §8 [critical].** §8 delays the effective date 180 days, but §5(a) applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment," and §3 has no effective date of its own. The two provisions disagree about when liability begins. Choose one trigger and key every provision to it.

3. **§3(b) [critical].** The grandfather clause exempts any mining under an exploration license issued before enactment, with no limit on volume, duration, area, or purpose. Exploration authority could be used for full commercial recovery, and the cutoff invites a rush of new licenses between introduction and enactment. Limit the exemption to activities within the license's stated exploration scope, cap volume, add a sunset, and set the cutoff at the introduction date.

4. **§3(c) [critical].** The environmental-assessment exemption has no limit on volume, duration, or sale of recovered minerals, and no agency approval is required. Commercial recovery can be relabeled as assessment. Require advance agency approval, a volume cap, a bar on sale or export of recovered material, and public reporting. "Environmental assessment" is also a NEPA term of art, so define it for this Act.

5. **§3(b).** "Exploration license" is undefined and doesn't name the issuing law or body. It's unclear whether it covers permits under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) and whether it reaches exploration contracts that the International Seabed Authority issues to sponsored companies, which are contracts rather than licenses. Define the term by reference to specific authorizations.

6. **§2(1)(A).** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel and per year. Operators can split work across several vessels, each under the threshold, or spread recovery over multiple years. Measure the threshold per operation or project and add a cumulative multi-year count.

7. **§2(1)(A).** "Recovery" is measured in metric tons without saying whether that means wet or dry weight, ore or nodules, or mass before or after sediment removal. Operators can choose a measurement method to stay under the threshold. Specify dry mass of material brought aboard.

8. **§2(1)(A).** It's unclear whether "depths greater than 200 meters" refers to water depth or seabed depth. Clarify the measurement point.

9. **§2(1)(A).** "Other mineral resources" is undefined, so it's unclear whether sand, gravel, aggregates, phosphorites, cobalt crusts, and hydrothermal sulfides are covered. Define "mineral resources" and list the covered categories.

10. **§2(1)(B).** "The Secretary" is undefined. Which department? Since §4 refers to NOAA, the Act should say so.

11. **§2(1)(B).** "Determines" and "comparable" are undefined, and the Secretary has no criteria, procedure, notice requirement, or deadline. A Secretary could decline to act, and the determination may not be reviewable. Add ecological harm criteria, a public determination process, and a deadline.

12. **§2(2).** The U.S. person definition excludes LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies. A U.S. firm could mine through a Marshall Islands or Cayman subsidiary and fall outside §3(a). Add a control or beneficial-ownership test that covers all entity forms, and define "State" (including whether DC and the territories count).

13. **§2 (general).** "Person" is not defined. Clarify that it includes entities, officers, and individuals, and whether it reaches employees working on foreign-flagged vessels.

14. **§3(a).** "Engage in" is undefined. It doesn't clearly reach financing, insurance, vessel construction, equipment supply, or processing, so a company could fund or supply offshore mining without violating the Act. Define the term to cover these activities, using a knowledge standard where appropriate.

15. **§3(a).** The prohibition doesn't cover importing, buying, or selling minerals mined abroad, so companies could mine offshore and bring the product into the U.S. Add an import and sale prohibition for minerals from covered mining.

16. **§3(a).** Extraterritorial reach is limited to U.S. persons, so a foreign-flagged vessel with no U.S. persons aboard is outside the Act. Add port-access and services restrictions for vessels engaged in covered mining, and address the reach over the EEZ and high seas expressly.

17. **§3(a).** "In the United States" is undefined. Clarify whether it includes the EEZ, the continental shelf, and the outer continental shelf.

18. **No savings or relationship clause.** The Act doesn't say how it interacts with DSHMRA, OCSLA, ESA, MMPA, NEPA, or the Clean Water Act. Industry will argue that the prohibition conflicts with existing authorizations, so state whether the Act repeals, amends, or supersedes DSHMRA permits and pending applications.

19. **§4(a).** "Operator" is undefined. "Register" has no deadline, no required content, and no provision on whether the registry is public, and there's no penalty for failing to register.

20. **§4 (scope mismatch).** Registration and reporting apply only to "covered vessels" over 5,000 gross tons, but §3 prohibits any operation that exceeds the 10,000-ton threshold. A smaller vessel can be prohibited under §3 yet never register or report, so the reporting can't verify compliance. Align the definitions or extend reporting to any vessel conducting recovery.

21. **§2(3) and §4(a).** "Equipped for the recovery" is vague and can be avoided by retrofitting or by reconfiguring equipment. Define covered equipment by function (collectors, risers, lift systems).

22. **§4(b).** Reports have no required content (tonnage, location, depth, sediment plume, discharges), no deadline, no verification right, and no public release. "Certified by the operator" carries no false-statement penalty. Specify content, deadlines, penalties for false certification, and public posting.

23. **§4 (general).** There's no inspection, boarding, monitoring (AIS/VMS), or recordkeeping authority. Without these, reporting is self-reported and can't be checked. Add them.

24. **§5 (general).** No agency is designated to enforce the Act, and no one is authorized to bring civil actions. Name the enforcing agency and DOJ's role, and address Coast Guard support.

25. **§5(a).** It's unclear whether a continuing violation accrues per day, per vessel, per ton, or per operation. The provision also has no minimum penalty, no disgorgement of profits, no forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or minerals, and no inflation adjustment. Define "violation" and add forfeiture and disgorgement.

26. **§5 (enforcement tools).** There's no citizen-suit provision and no express authority for injunctions or restoration. Enforcement depends entirely on the government. Add a citizen-suit provision and explicit injunctive and restoration remedies, and state the limitations period (absent a provision, the default for civil penalties is five years under 28 U.S.C. 2462).

27. **§5(b).** "Willfully" is undefined. The provision doesn't address responsible corporate officers, aiding and abetting, conspiracy, or criminal jurisdiction over conduct abroad. Add these.

28. **§6.** "Shall seek to negotiate" requires no particular result, report, or consequence, and "equivalent to those in section 3" is undefined, so a much weaker treaty could satisfy it. Require a report to Congress, define minimum standards, and state what happens to the Act if a treaty enters into force.

29. **§7(a).** Nothing requires the NASEM report to be commissioned, produced, or delivered, and no deadline is set. Congress could act without the report, or the report might never be produced. Require the report and set a deadline.

30. **§7(a).** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the provision doesn't say who bears the burden of proof. Define the standard and place the burden on the party seeking to lift the prohibition.

31. **§7(a).** A joint resolution goes to the President and can be vetoed, and courts won't review it. Clarify the procedure, including whether it's an ordinary bill and whether expedited consideration applies.

32. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes one provision, such as the U.S. person definition or the §2(1)(B) delegation, the rest may fall with it. Add a severability clause.

33. **No rulemaking authority.** The Act doesn't authorize the Secretary or NOAA to issue regulations for reporting forms, determinations, or enforcement procedures. Add explicit rulemaking authority.

34. **§§4, 3(b), 6, 7(b), 8 (timeline).** Registration, grandfathering, the treaty deadline, the sunset, and the effective date are keyed to different triggers (enactment, effective date, introduction) with no reconciliation. Define the key dates in one place and tie each deadline to one of them.

If you'd like, I can draft replacement language for the critical items (1 through 4) so you can bring them to the markup.
